sweep_summary: Naro (naro1249) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's single title hit, Schmidt 1986 (Khoisan folklore, Festschrift Lorna Marshall), is a false positive on 'feet' and irrelevant to word stress. Beyond the listed item, I downloaded and read the two open first-hand Naro sources that exist: Kagaya 1978 'A phonetic sketch of Naron around Ghanzi' (TUFS repository scan, scanned) and Visser's 2022 Apeldoorn dissertation on Naro PGN-markers; both describe Naro as a three-register-tone language (H/M/L; Kagaya: high/mid/low plus high-falling) and neither says a word about stress or accent placement. Bleek 1956's Bushman Dictionary (archive.org) is likewise silent for Naron. No first-hand stress statement for Naro was read, so no new stress statement was found. The likely places for one remain unread: Visser 1998 'The phonological system of Naro' (Koppe, print only; high priority), Visser 2013 'Naro' in Vossen's The Khoesan Languages (Routledge, DOI 10.4324/9780203084465, paywalled; high), Bleek 1928 'The Naron' (HathiTrust full view exists but is could not be reached by automated download; medium) and Barnard 1985 Nharo wordlist (print only; medium).org, Open Library, HathiTrust dump, and the TUA repository.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Naro is described as a register-tone language: every syllabic vowel or nasal carries one of three tonemes (H, M, L), and disyllabic/bimoraic words show one of seven lexical tone melodies (HH, HL, MM, ML, LH, LM, LL). Neither Visser 2013 (visible snippets), Visser 2022 (full text), Kagaya 1978 (full text), Bleek 1928 (full-text index) nor Barnard 1985 (snippets) says anything about word stress or accent placement; no source states that stress exists, where it falls, or that it is absent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal only: Visser 2013 p. 98 notes a consonant-conditioned constraint ('.. the tone on the first vowel is low. The only exceptions that have been found so far are bóò "to see" (cf. Proto-Bantu *-bón-) and biû "milk"'); Visser 2022 §3.3.12 gives the predictable tone of PGN enclitics (H after MM/ML/LM hosts, L after HH/HL/LH/LL hosts). The word 'stress' on p. 98 ('.. stress (see Vossen 2004)') belongs to the preceding Khwe/Kalahari-Khoe section, not to Naro.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word level (tone melodies of two-TBU words) plus the prosodic unit noun/verb + PGN enclitic; citation forms in Visser's practical orthography (acute = H, grave = L, mid unmarked).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, Naro (naro1249): Visser's Naro of D'Kar/Gantsi (Ghanzi District, Botswana), Kagaya's 'Naron around Ghanzi', Barnard's 'Nharo' and Bleek's 'Naron' (Sandfontein/Gobabis area, 1920s). No dialect-specific claims; Vossen 2022 'ǂHaba' (Glottolog-listed) is a separate Kalahari Khoe variety and was not examined.

sources.quote: Most of words collected in this study consist of one to three syllables, words consisting of more than three syllables are rare, except in compounded words. [...] The duration of vowel seems to depend mainly on the context of the word, i.e, when the word is pronounced in isolation, the duration of the vowel terminating the word tends to be long and when it is pronounced sentence-medially, the same vowel tends to be short. (The vowel also tends to become long when it has a contour tone.)
sources.note: Read in full (35 pp., scanned). Covers syllable structure (V, CV, N), vowels, clicks, consonants and register tones (high/mid/low, high-falling); no statement about word stress or accent anywhere in the paper. Silent on stress.
